title: Ex-White House AI adviser weighs in on national security as Huang is back as Nvidia CEO
description: Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang is back in leadership after resigning recently. Ben Buchanan, a Biden administration AI adviser, discusses what that me
body:
Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang is back in leadership after resigning recently. Ben Buchanan, a Biden administration AI adviser, discusses what that means for U.S. national security and chip exports.   

    
        
          Transcript
        
    SCOTT DETROW, HOST:  We're going to stay on this topic. The Nvidia board said that it, quote, "received input from senior levels of the United States government" and is, quote, "confident that Mr. Huang's reinstatement poses no national security risk." President Trump has said that basically meant him, that he gave this input to the Nvidia board. We're going to talk this through with a former White House official. Ben Buchanan was special adviser for artificial intelligence during the Biden administration. Welcome to ALL THINGS CONSIDERED.BEN BUCHANAN: Thanks for having me.DETROW: What do you make of the White House's direct involvement here?BUCHANAN: I'm surprised. Certainly, I was in the White House when Sam Altman had his firing and reinstatement, and I got a lot of questions then about, was the White House involved? And our posture was we did not want to live in a world in which the White House had roles in picking the executives of American companies. So it's certainly a departure from past norms in that regard.DETROW: Yeah. I mean, there's a lot to ask about here. But I'm curious, from your past perspective as a White House official on this topic, is Nvidia as indispensable as it has been made out to be when it comes to the AI landscape, when it comes to the national security side of that?BUCHANAN: Nvidia and their chips are absolutely incredibly important. To me, though, that reaffirms the importance of making sure those chips don't go to China more so than it reaffirms the importance of any one particular person. So my hope here is that because this technology matters so much, that Congress does a full investigation into the national security stakes of this, including were these chips being smuggled, was China accessing them remotely through data centers in Southeast Asia and the like? To me, that is really the crux of the national security matter in this instance.DETROW: I want to go to the national security question at the heart of the Huang storyline. This is the reporting of this alleged relationship with an alleged Chinese espionage asset. What do you make of that particular part of the story?BUCHANAN: It's hard to say from this vantage point of what's true and who knew what. Certainly, there's a lot of reporting that does seem to be credible that she was in the middle of chip smuggling and perhaps also had a relationship or ongoing conversations with the Ministry of State Security in China. To me, the chip smuggling part is enough reason for serious concern, and the intelligence links are secondary.DETROW: What is the best way to frame how policy has changed from the Biden administration to the Trump administration when it comes to the accessibility of these chips in other countries, particularly China? Because that is an area where there's been a lot of reporting that Huang and Nvidia have had a lot of influence on President Trump.BUCHANAN: We came into office in 2021 with the conviction that AI was going to get very powerful and that it would matter for national security and that it was chips, including Nvidia's chips, that were driving that increase in power. For that reason, in 2022, and then each subsequent year thereafter, we implemented and then tightened a series of export controls, denying China access to those chips and cutting off China smuggling routes and access to remote data centers in places like Singapore, containing those chips.President Trump, when he came into office in 2025, walked back or declined to enforce a number of those policies - after initially talking and acting tough, walked those policies back in the late spring and summer of 2025 and then into the fall of 2025. To his credit, as this scandal broke, last week President Trump did put some rules back in place that, so far as we can tell, are still on the books that go back to something closer to the Biden administration policy.DETROW: So when it comes to the policy of all of this, what do you think it may mean going forward if Jensen Huang is back in this perch with President Trump's full support, given the way that the two of them seem to have talked about these policies?BUCHANAN: It really depends on what Congress does here. And because of President Trump's walk-back on this policy during his first two years, there has been a bipartisan move in Congress, including from some very MAGA senators - folks like Pete Ricketts and Jim Banks and Tom Cotton - to tighten the export controls once more, this time through legislation, depriving the administration of the opportunity to change these policies back and forth. Those bills - the MATCH Act, the OVERWATCH Act - are the two big ones -  have bipartisan support, I think have a good chance of passing this Congress. And some of the leaders of those bills have come out today after this news and said they still have a lot of questions for Jensen, and they seem committed still to implementing this policy fully.DETROW: That's Ben Buchanan, professor at Johns Hopkins University and a former AI adviser to the Biden White House. His new book about all of this is called "The Bitter Struggle." Thanks so much.BUCHANAN: Thanks for having me.

title: Republican wants FBI and CIA answers before questioning Nvidia chief
description:
Rep. Brian Fitzpatrick, R-Penn., on Nvidia CEO's upcoming House committee interview
    
            
                
                T
body:
Rep. Brian Fitzpatrick, R-Penn., on Nvidia CEO's upcoming House committee interview
    
            
                
                Transcript
            
        
                Download
                
                
                    
                        
                            
                            Embed
                        
                        
                            <iframe src="https://www.npr.org/player/embed/nx-s1-6052417/nx-s1-10019261" width="100%" height="290" frameborder="0" scrolling="no" title="NPR embedded audio player">
                        
                    
                
                
                  
                    
                    Transcript
                  
                
        
    



      
            
        
            
            
            
        


    
        
                Rep. Brian Fitzpatrick, R-Pa., speaks at a House Foreign Affairs subcommittee hearing in Washington on Sept. 21, 2022.
                
                    Samuel Corum/Getty Images
                
                hide caption
            
            
    
        Samuel Corum/Getty Images
    

   
   Jensen Huang is back at the helm of Nvidia with President Trump's backing. But the questions surrounding the AI chipmaker and its ties to China are far from settled.   U.S. intelligence officials told congressional staff there is no evidence that Alice Huang, the woman who had an affair with the Nvidia chief, was a Chinese spy or intelligence asset, according to a person familiar with the matter who was granted anonymity to speak about a closed-door briefing.   There is also no evidence that she initiated the affair to collect intelligence for China's government, the person told NPR's Ryan Lucas on condition of anonymity because of the sensitive nature of the matter. She is, however, believed to have passed along information after the affair began.   
   Trump has said he helped arrange Huang's return as CEO, and Nvidia's board maintains that his reinstatement presents no national security risk. Some Republican lawmakers, however, want to understand how those conclusions were reached.   Speaking to Morning Edition on Wednesday, before NPR obtained the new information, Rep. Brian Fitzpatrick, R-Pa., said he wants to hear from the FBI and CIA before Huang appears before House lawmakers next week.   For Fitzpatrick, a former FBI special agent who sits on the House Intelligence Committee, the inquiry begins with what federal authorities knew and whether they warned the Nvidia chief of potential espionage threats.   "What briefings did they give? When did they give them?" he asked.   Huang's reinstatement, Fitzpatrick said, should not put those questions to rest.   "The public is rightly concerned, and they deserve answers," he said.   Fitzpatrick also wants to hear from Attorney General Todd Blanche, who on Tuesday described Nvidia as a good corporate citizen, and Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick, whose department faces questions over Nvidia's chip exports to China.   "Anytime you do an investigation, you follow the facts wherever they lead, and you report those facts with unimpeachable integrity," Fitzpatrick said. "You leave no stone unturned."   The debate over Huang's reinstatement extends beyond Washington.   
   In Silicon Valley, his return has alarmed women and advocates who have spent years pushing for a better workplace culture, renewing questions about the limits of executive accountability.   Listen to the full interview by clicking on the blue button above.   The radio interview was edited by Ally Schweitzer.

title: The U.S. government is investigating Iranian ties to as many as 50 hacked commercial vessels
description: In an aerial view, a container ship arri
body:
In an aerial view, a container ship arrives at the Port of Oakland on Oct. 10, 2025 in Oakland, Calif.
                
                    Justin Sullivan/Getty Images
                
                hide caption
            
            
    
        Justin Sullivan/Getty Images
    

   
   The U.S. government has intelligence suggesting that up to 50 commercial shipping vessels were recently compromised by cyberattacks, activity federal officials are investigating as potentially linked to Iran.   That's according to a U.S. official familiar with the matter who was not authorized to speak on the record, a former military cyber operator and an industry executive briefed on the attacks. The series of breaches was first reported by the The Wall Street Journal.   The attacks against the maritime sector, if officials' suspicions are correct, may be the latest example of Iranian cyberattacks against global critical infrastructure during the ongoing war with the United States.   
   NPR has reported that cybersecurity experts and U.S. officials believe Iranian hackers were responsible for a series of digital attacks against U.S. water treatment systems across the country in August as well as a pattern of attacks targeting refrigeration cooling systems that led to spoiled food at grocery stores on U.S. military bases and all across Europe as recently as early November.   The Coast Guard and the FBI first partnered in August to send a "highly specialized team" to board two different foreign commercial vessels "in the Gulf of America" heading to U.S. ports, according to a statement provided by the FBI and the Coast Guard. "The captain, crew, and shore-side corporate staff were critical partners in helping to ensure the threats were mitigated," according to the statement.   The FBI and Coast Guard press offices also told NPR that there are no current "reports of operational disruptions, vessel instability, physical danger to crews, or environmental impacts."   However, there are dozens more ships in international waters that the U.S. government believes have been compromised by hackers and many others who might be vulnerable to similar attacks.   
   According to the U.S. official familiar with the investigation, bad actors took advantage of known vulnerabilities in Fortinet FortiGate devices, which are frequently used in the maritime industry. The Coast Guard and FBI released a cyber bulletin in September warning the industry that bad actors were breaking into these devices, which help manage firewalls and virtual private networks. "Threat actors routinely scan for specific, unpatched vulnerabilities to gain a foothold," the bulletin read.   According to the U.S. official, in some cases, employees aboard the ships suspected something nefarious was going on when they noticed email disruptions or couldn't log in to their accounts, or, in at least one case, an extended communications blackout. The U.S. official declined to comment on how the U.S. government knows about the extent of breaches across the sector.   
   However, according to the U.S. official, hackers were able to break in using the Fortinet vulnerability and then pivot from the ships' IT systems over to their network of devices controlling physical processes on the ships, what's called operational technology.   
   The U.S. official said the bad actors "could have impacted the systems on board that control propulsion, steering, navigation, and cargo management," though they did not share any examples of that kind of activity occurring. In at least one case, one of the ships affected was an LNG tanker designed to transport liquified natural gas. It's important to keep systems at a certain temperature to prevent dangerous accidents if a ship's cargo includes explosive materials –from chemicals to fuel.   While commercial vessels are accustomed to physical security reviews entering the United States following the Sept. 11 terrorist attacks, digital threats are becoming all the more important to track as adversaries can break in and cause damage from afar. "It's a totally new paradigm that these tankers are networked in this way," the U.S. official said.   Even so, national security officials have feared something like this might happen for years. A former Navy official who requested anonymity to discuss internal operations tells NPR that "we had been tracking the possibility to exploit and take control of [operational technology] systems on Navy ships and Merchant [Marine] ships for a long time, and now this is coming to fruition."   While the U.S. government is wary of advertising Iranian hacking efforts during the war, officials also want to spread awareness of the vulnerability of internet connected devices, particularly those that are linked to the technology that controls critical processes. "These are not sophisticated attacks," the official said. "This is a known vulnerability that could be mitigated with some pretty basic cyber hygiene."   
   "Modern ships are highly integrated systems. A cyberattack presents significant risks, including the potential for a collision, grounding, oil spill, or even an explosion. The Coast Guard regularly publishes bulletins on cyber vulnerabilities and actions vessel owners and operators can take to secure their networks," according to a statement from the Coast Guard.   Ahead of the winter and a busy holiday season for commercial shipping, officials are bracing themselves to investigate any ship entering U.S. ports that could be compromised.   "People never think about what a modern blessing electricity is until it goes out. People take the marine transportation system for granted until there's a problem and their stuff doesn't get there by Christmas," the U.S. official said. "I wish more Americans knew how complex this system is."

title: Democrats probe whether Trump Jr.-aligned businesses benefit from government access
description: Donald Trump Jr. speaks on stage on the
body:
Donald Trump Jr. speaks on stage on the second day of the 2026 Republican National Convention on Sept. 10, in Dallas.
                
                    Brandon Bell/Getty Images
                
                hide caption
            
            
    
        Brandon Bell/Getty Images
    

   
   Congressional Democrats, led by likely House Judiciary Committee Chair Rep. Jamie Raskin of Maryland, are expanding their investigation into the investment firm 1789 Capital, which brought on Donald Trump Jr. as a partner days after his father's reelection to the White House.   Since then, investigators say the firm has grown from "a middling venture capital firm" with $150 million in managed assets to "the darling of the venture capital world" with $3 billion in managed assets.   Investigators want to determine whether the growth was boosted by the president's son leveraging political influence or government information to secure federal contracts and regulatory changes for companies with connections to the investment firm.   
   Trump Jr. told Axios last week that the timing of his hiring at 1789 Capital was coincidental, noting that he had already been working with founder Omeed Malik for years. He also said he draws a clear line when marketing and raising money for the firm.   "I make it very clear [to foreign investors] that I have nothing to do with government," Trump Jr. said. "[The president is] my father, but he's also busy and I probably haven't spoken to him in three weeks."   He also suggested he doesn't use or need government connections to make smart investments. "Trying to do the things that we're alleged to be doing every day, I think that would last for about two seconds before it was out there very publicly," Trump Jr. said. He added that the firm relies on teams of analysts to make investments in industries where there are obvious public and national security demands but relatively few companies who are able to meet those needs.   NPR reached out to Donald Trump Jr. for comment and did not hear back.   Regarding Raskin's request for documents from 1789 Capital, Bill Burck, an attorney representing the firm, told NPR, "We responded to Congressman Raskin back in September pointing out in detail the many flaws in his understanding of how 1789 has operated and a number of basic factual errors. He never bothered to reply. Facts are facts and Congressman Raskin has them wrong here but persists in his tall tales against 1789. These are personal attacks untethered to actual evidence."   
   What investigators are interested in   On Monday, congressional investigators sent letters to four companies — military contractor Hadrian, electronic cigarette company Juul, prediction market Polymarket and online weapons dealer GrabAGun — asking them to preserve their records and turn over a broad array of records to the committee.   The committee is interested in Hadrian's contracts with the armed forces, signed in March of this year, worth close to a billion dollars. Investigators allege that, in 2024, the company had a single manufacturing facility and "no history of fulfilling government contracts." They also noted that CEO Chris Power donated tens of thousands of dollars to Trump-aligned political organizations in advance of the 2024 election.   Political donations are constitutionally-protected speech and not necessarily evidence of wrongdoing. 1789 Capital first invested in Hadrian in July 2025. The company is also backed by a number of bluechip investors, including Morgan Stanley, T. Rowe Price, Andreessen Horowitz and JPMorganChase. Hadrian did not reply to a request for comment from NPR.   Investigators also allege that Trump Jr.'s firm took a stake in e-cigarette company Juul in March 2025, as the company teetered near insolvency following rulings during the first Trump administration limiting the sale of various flavor cartridges. Four months after that investment, though before it was publicly disclosed, investigators say the company's fortunes rebounded after the Trump administration authorized five new Juul e-cigarette products. The company has announced plans for more flavor authorization applications moving forward.   In a statement to NPR, a Juul spokesperson said the company had received Rep. Raskin's letter and are "reviewing it closely. As always, we intend to cooperate with any Congressional effort to understand our company, our commitment to combating underage vaping, and our mission to help adult smokers of combustible cigarettes transition completely away from smoking."   Investigators are also interested in betting site Polymarket. They say that following a meeting between Polymarket leadership and Trump Jr. at the 2024 Republican National Convention, 1789 Capital invested in the company — which at the time was banned in the United States. In July 2025, after President Trump took office, the Justice Department and the Commodity Futures Trading Commission notified the company that they had closed investigations launched during the Biden administration, according to reporting from Bloomberg News. The CFTC later authorized a U.S. version of the platform to launch. Investigators allege 1789's investment resulted in a 70-fold return.   
   GrabAGun, a company that "believe[s] people should be able to use their computers, phones, and tablets to shop for firearms the same way they purchase everything else," became, according to investigators, a publicly-traded company with the help of 1789 Capital leadership, including Trump Jr., who serves of its board.   In May 2026, the Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms and Explosives (ATF) proposed a draft rule that would make it easier to ship guns directly to people's homes. At the time, GrabAGun claimed that the company is "uniquely positioned to capitalize on this potential opportunity." Investigators are seeking to understand what knowledge and involvement Trump Jr. had of the proposed rule change.   In a statement to NPR, GrabAGun said the investigators' letter is "a political document, and its allegations are baseless." It added that the ATF's review of its regulations was well known across the firearms industry, and the agency published numerous proposed rules for public comment.   "GrabAGun's only input came through public comments on several of those proposals," the company said.

title: California Democrat Rep. Gomez resigns following ethics report on sexual misconduct allegations
description: U.S. Rep. Jimmy Gomez, seen here at a Co
body:
U.S. Rep. Jimmy Gomez, seen here at a Congressional hearing in March, announced Monday that he would resign following a report from the House Ethics committee on allegations of sexual misconduct.
                
                    Heather Diehl/Getty Images North America
                
                hide caption
            
            
    
        Heather Diehl/Getty Images North America
    

   
   Rep. Jimmy Gomez, D-Calif., says he is resigning from Congress after a bipartisan investigation released Monday found "substantial evidence" he engaged in sexual misconduct toward a House staffer.   The House Ethics Committee concluded Gomez violated House rules by "making unwelcome sexual advances and engaging in unwelcome sexual conduct towards a House staffer and disregarding the power imbalance inherent in his relationship with House staffers."   The report also says the behavior could constitute criminal sexual assault.   Gomez has served in Congress since 2017 representing parts of Los Angeles. He lost reelection this fall to fellow Democrat Angela Gonzales-Torres. California uses a system where the top two vote-getters no matter the party advance to the general election. Gomez says his resignation will be effective Dec. 1.   
   Lisa Banks and Sarah Nesbitt, attorneys for the unnamed House staffer, wrote in a statement that their client testified to the committee truthfully and at personal risk.   "She sacrificed her own sense of safety and privacy to help reveal the ongoing misogyny and debauchery that permeates Capitol Hill," Banks and Nesbitt wrote. "Representative Gomez seems to believe that the power he wields, both as a man and as a member of Congress, makes him untouchable. Today's findings are a meaningful step toward dismantling that belief."   In a statement announcing his plan to resign, Gomez wrote that he cooperated with the investigation, but has strong disagreements with the report and its conclusions.   "Among other significant deficiencies and omissions, the report does not include key portions of my testimony that are essential to a full and fair understanding of what occurred," he wrote.   "I also have serious concerns about the process. In my interview, I answered the Committee's questions only to see my statements selectively quoted, disparaged, and disregarded throughout the final report, to which I was given no opportunity to respond."   
   The House Ethics Committee, which includes five Democrats and five Republicans, opened its investigation into Gomez in August following a press report of Gomez kissing a staffer from another Congressional office at a party. Gomez denied those allegations.   The committee asked Gomez to disclose whether he "ever engaged in a romantic or sexual relationship or made sexual contact with a congressional staffer." Gomez disclosed interactions with two women — telling the committee the encounters were all consensual. Both women spoke to the committee.   
   One denied "she had ever had a nonconsensual sexual encounter" with Gomez. The other, described as Witness 1 in the report, said she had more than one encounter with Gomez and she did not consider them consensual.   She told investigators that Gomez made sexual contact without her consent at a bar in February 2024 and then was forceful with her and tried to kiss her at his congressional office in July 2024.   Gomez denied the interactions were nonconsensual. The staffer, described as Witness 1 in the committee report, eventually left her job on Capitol Hill.   "Here, the House lost Witness 1 as a competent and able staffer because of Representative Gomez's misconduct and because of a broader culture of disrespect and toxic sexual behavior toward staff that permeates life on the Hill and is long overdue for correction," the committee wrote.   The report comes amid a broader conversation about how Congress deals with the behavior of its members, especially when it comes to sexual misconduct.   In April, Democrat Eric Swalwell of California resigned his House seat amid allegations of sexual assault and misconduct. He also denied the allegations. Rep. Tony Gonzales (R-Tex.) also resigned from the House after admitting to an affair with a former staff member.   Rep. Chuck Edwards (R-N.C.) dropped his reelection bid earlier this year after the House Ethics Committee recommended he face a censure vote for allegedly harassing two young female staffers. Edwards denied the allegations.   Republican Reps. Max Miller of Ohio and Cory Mills of Florida also face House Ethics investigations stemming from allegations of domestic violence. Both deny wrongdoing.   Miller lost his reelection bid this fall and Mills lost his GOP primary.   Last week, the House Ethics Committee adopted new rules with the aim of speeding up investigations into sexual misconduct and improving transparency.

title: Trump takes credit for Jensen Huang returns to Nvidia, says its good for the economy
description: President Trump touted the return of Jensen Huang to Nvidia's C-suite as good for the company — and good for the United States economy.
body:
President Trump touted the return of Jensen Huang to Nvidia's C-suite as good for the company — and good for the United States economy.   

    
        
          Transcript
        
    MICHEL MARTIN, HOST:  Jensen Huang is back as CEO of Nvidia less than two weeks after resigning, a return that President Trump helped engineer and is now celebrating.STEVE INSKEEP, HOST:  Huang and the president have been allies. His company donated to the new White House ballroom. Huang also routinely advised the president on AI policy. He will surely face questions about that relationship and much more when he attends a closed-door interview that three House committees have planned for next week. In a moment, we bring in Representative Raja Krishnamoorthi, who's on two of those panels. We begin with the news.MARTIN: White House correspondent Danielle Kurtzleben has been covering this. Good morning.DANIELLE KURTZLEBEN, BYLINE: Good morning.MARTIN: So what has the president had to say about his role in all of this Nvidia situation?KURTZLEBEN: Well, shortly after the announcement of the reinstatement, the president posted that this was for the good not only of Nvidia, but the U.S. economy. And then yesterday morning, he did a 50-minute phone interview with CNBC. And Trump was asked if he directly called into the Nvidia board meeting, and he demurred, but he did make it clear that he pushed the company on this decision. He said he convinced them - his words. He went on to say that he was able to convince Nvidia because the company's stock had plummeted following Huang's ouster, and that was again after the news initially broke that Huang was having an affair with an alleged spy for China.MARTIN: Now, let me just pause here because I'm not sure that - perhaps if people don't cover the business world, etc., they might not know that it is very extraordinary for a White House to weigh in on private business decisions.KURTZLEBEN: Yeah. It's a huge deal. Even if it's not really unusual for this White House to intervene in the economy and even private businesses, this White House has taken stakes in dozens of companies, for example. Plus, Trump has gotten very cozy with the tech world, with CEOs showing up to White House events or donating to his ballroom. But beyond all that, it really stood out to me this thing that Trump did yesterday - he posted this meme playing off that famous picture of him after he was shot in Butler, Pennsylvania. In this new picture, it's Huang, not Trump, raising his fist with blood spattered on his face. And in that fist is a red bra, referencing, of course, Huang's affair. Now, this is the president of the United States posting this, and it's trolling. And also it's once again celebrating a private business decision.MARTIN: Extraordinary. That image is extraordinary. But why was the president so dead set on getting Huang back into his CEO role?KURTZLEBEN: Well, Trump told CNBC he was concerned that Chinese president Xi Jinping might lure Huang over to China to boost their chip business. But also let's remember Trump loves to talk about the stock market. Even when other economic measures aren't looking great, he often has stock indexes to talk about. So he told CNBC the Huang decision not only turned Nvidia's stock around, but maybe the whole market after what was a rough week for stocks.(SOUNDBITE OF ARCHIVED RECORDING)PRESIDENT DONALD TRUMP: I watched the screen, and I said, boy, that thing's like a rocket ship going in the wrong direction. Now it's a rocket ship going in the right direction, and it's taken the whole market with it.UNIDENTIFIED PERSON: It's just an incredible turnaround.TRUMP: Well, I don't know.UNIDENTIFIED PERSON: You've been watching corporate America...TRUMP: There could be - it could be that there's never been anything like it, actually.KURTZLEBEN: One other important point here - the president has been trading in Nvidia stock, as we know from his financial disclosures. In early September, there was a purchase he made worth up to a quarter of a million dollars. And this is also part of a pattern of trading in companies by the president that also are affected by his administration's actions.MARTIN: OK. The national security issues. What is the status of that? It strikes me that those issues have not been resolved. Have they?KURTZLEBEN: No, those aren't gone. Now, Trump said on CNBC that the White House investigated this, and he's not concerned about Huang from a security perspective. But we do know that Secretary of State Marco Rubio wrote a memo earlier this year warning that Huang was having this relationship. And yesterday, Nebraska Republican Senator Pete Ricketts posted that Huang's behavior doesn't support reinstatement, and he said he looks forward to Huang's scheduled testimony before the Senate in December. And that's meaningful for someone from the president's own party to differ with him on this. So we will see how many join that charge and how vocal they are.MARTIN: That is NPR's Danielle Kurtzleben. Danielle, thank you.KURTZLEBEN: Thank you.

title: Group of Senate Democrats push to add freshman to leadership
description: U.S. Senate Majority Leader Charles Schu
body:
U.S. Senate Majority Leader Charles Schumer (D-NY), center, is seen here meeting with newly elected Democratic Senators, (L-R) Senator-elect Andy Kim (D-NJ), Senator-elect Ruben Gallego (D-AZ), Senator-elect Angela Alsobrooks (D-MD) Senator-elect Adam Schiff (D-CA) Senator-elect Lisa Blunt Rochester (D-DE) and Senator-elect Elissa Slotkin (D-MI) at the U.S. Capitol Building on November 12, 2024. That group of senators is pushing to add an incoming freshman senator to the leadership ranks.
                
                    Chip Somodevilla/Getty Images/Getty Images North America
                
                hide caption
            
            
    
        Chip Somodevilla/Getty Images/Getty Images North America
    

   
   A group of Senate Democrats elected in 2024 sent a letter to colleagues Tuesday proposing to add an incoming freshman to the leadership ranks.    "The Freshman Representative to Leadership would be elected by members of the incoming freshman class and confirmed by the Conference," the letter said. "We intend to request a vote on this proposal."    The letter, first reported by Politico, is signed by California Sen. Adam Schiff, Maryland Sen. Angela Alsobrooks, Michigan Sen. Elissa Slotkin, Arizona Sen. Ruben Gallego, Delaware Sen. Lisa Blunt Rochester, and New Jersey Sen. Andy Kim.    The letter nods to the diverse class of incoming freshmen who helped catapult the party to controlling both chambers of Congress.    
   "These freshmen have their fingers on the pulse of long-time Democratic voters, those who voted for Democrats for the first time this past Election Day, and everyone in-between," the letter reads. "The deserve a seat at the table."    Senate Democrats have been signaling a desire to uplift new voices in the party.   "On election night, people voted very clearly for a new generation of leadership. That was very, very clear," Slotkin said during remarks at a conference of Democrats after the midterms.    New Jersey Sen. Cory Booker told MS NOW  that leadership extends beyond the top post.    "This is a time for new leadership," Booker said, mentioning wanting to see more of incoming Sens. Annie Andrews of South Carolina and James Talarico of Texas. "I want to see them out front, I want to see them taking issues, I want to see them running on the field."   The proposed rule change comes ahead of the leadership election next week. Maryland Sen. Chris Van Hollen is challenging Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer, D-N.Y., for the majority leader.    Senate leadership is comprised not only of the top position of Majority leader but of additional conference officers. Both Van Hollen and Schumer support the idea of adding a position for a freshman to that leadership group.    
   "Leader Schumer was already planning to do this and is incredibly supportive of the idea," a spokesperson told NPR.    On Tuesday, Van Hollen posted to social media: "There should be a freshman senator on the Senate leadership team. As I've said, we need a new way to organize so we can deliver for the American people."

title: For workplace culture champions, Jensen Huang's return is 'unfathomable'
description: Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang speaks to media
body:
Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang speaks to media after a roundtable with South Korean AI and robotics startups on June 8, 2026, in Seoul, South Korea.
                
                    Chung Sung-Jun/Getty Images AsiaPac
                
                hide caption
            
            
    
        Chung Sung-Jun/Getty Images AsiaPac
    

   
   Sign up for NPR's Up First morning newsletter for the stories you need to start your day.      On Monday morning, a couple hours after Nvidia's board announced it had reinstated co-founder Jensen Huang as CEO, President Trump shared an AI-generated image on social media.   It's based on that striking photo of the president from 2024, just after he survived an assasination attempt. Surrounded by Secret Service agents, his face bloodied, Trump hoists a defiant fist in the air.   In the doctored photo, instead of Trump, it's Huang. An Nvidia flag flies behind him. And in his hoisted fist, he holds a red bra.   
   "I was absolutely flabbergasted," says Bo Young Lee, who worked as chief diversity officer at Uber for five years starting in 2018.   
   To Lee, it seems Trump is suggesting that the Nvidia CEO is as important to the country as he is.   "But then also the red bra is an indication that it's open hunting season for women," she says. "It stirs up all sorts of stereotypes and misogynistic perspectives about women."   To others, the image drives home the idea that in Silicon Valley, as long as you're successful, anything goes.   The White House has not responded to NPR's questions about what Trump was trying to say with the image.   Spy intrigue overshadows workplace transgressions   Even as Huang's return to Nvidia has been cheered by investors, some employees and Trump, it has sparked shock and disbelief among others, including those who have long worked to improve workplace culture in Silicon Valley.   "It's actually unfathomable to me," says Lee, who now serves as an adviser to AI4ALL, a nonprofit dedicated to increasing diversity, inclusion, and responsible practices in artificial intelligence.   After The New York Times revealed that Huang had engaged in an extramarital affair with a woman the U.S government believes is a Chinese intelligence asset, Lee watched as the broader conversation was dominated by concerns about national security, corporate governance and Nvidia's stock price.   
   That scandal overshadowed allegations of other problematic behavior in the workplace, specifically Huang's alleged affair with Kimberly Powell, Nvidia's vice president of healthcare, one of Huang's many direct reports.   "Everyone is minimizing that alleged relationship there because of who she is," says Lee.   The fact that Powell is herself a senior leader who makes a lot of money shouldn't matter, Lee says. She argues that people in subordinate roles, even powerful ones, can't properly consent, "simply for the fact that there is this power differential."   Nvidia's board did find that Huang's behavior was "inconsistent" with the company's code of conduct. By Monday morning, that didn't seem to matter.   "The Board of Directors voted unanimously to reinstate Mr. Huang following a series of discussions and meetings with Mr. Huang, after which the Board was satisfied with respect to Mr. Huang's candor and ability to lead Nvidia," the board said in a statement.   
   Lee says that response sends a message to Nvidia employees and all of Silicon Valley that it's OK to break the rules as long as you come clean.   "'Just be transparent with us,'" she imagines the board saying.   Nvidia did not respond to NPR's questions about Lee's concerns.   A deepening of "tech bro" culture in Trump's second term   In Silicon Valley, there have been private conversations about Huang's alleged workplace transgressions and the power dynamics at play, but women don't appear eager to speak publicly.   NPR reached out to two dozen women who work in the tech space. Freada Kapor Klein was one of the few willing to talk. The social impact investor says conversations about workplace behavior are much quieter than they have been in other eras, such as in 2017 and 2018, when a number of venture capitalists resigned amid allegations they were sexually harassing female entrepreneurs.   In 2017, Kapor Klein and her husband, Mitch Kapor, used their positions as early investors in Uber to publicly call out the company over its toxic culture, one they said tolerated bullying and harassment. The co-founder and CEO Travis Kalanick ended up resigning. Kapor Klein hoped it'd be a teachable moment.   
   But now, she feels Silicon Valley has gone backwards.   "Tech bro culture is stronger now than I have seen it in decades," she says, adding that Trump's attacks on DEI have amplified that culture.   Among women and people of color in Silicon Valley, she says there's now real trepidation about the anti-DEI sentiment — the axing of programs, chief diversity officers and employee resource groups.   "All of the supports or mechanisms have been pretty much stripped away," she says.   
            
        
            
            
            
        


    
        
                Screens display news of the reinstatement of Jensen Huang, seen outside the NASDAQ MarketSite, in New York, on November 23, 2026.
                
                    Angela Weiss/AFP via Getty Images
                
                hide caption
            
            
    
        Angela Weiss/AFP via Getty Images
    

   
   "All that matters is money"   To be clear, Huang has not been accused of predatory behavior. Still, Kapor Klein says his swift comeback is troubling.   "It is a resounding message that all that matters is money," she says. "If you are thought of as a singular talent, you can violate corporate policy, you can possibly threaten national security, you can make up your own rules as you go, you can create toxic workplace culture — as long as you bring in the money."   By the end of last week, Nvidia's stock had fallen almost 49% from its peak in October, and about 27% from before Huang's resignation. On Monday, it rebounded significantly.   Lee says Silicon Valley has always had an unhealthy relationship with its "genius founders."   "We elevate these leaders to god-like levels, and that's been done to Mark Zuckerberg, and that's being done to Sam Altman, and that's definitely [been] done to Jensen Huang," says Lee. "You become untouchable at that point."   Kapor Klein says what's unfolded at Nvidia has made abundantly clear that AI companies need guardrails for their CEOs, not just for the tools they're creating.   "We see a board that ignored that," she says. "There are no guardrails on this CEO's behavior."   NPR's Scott Horsley contributed to this story.

schema.headline: For workplace culture champions, Jensen Huang's return is 'unfathomable'

title: Jensen Huang returns to Nvidia. And, Rep. Gomez resigns amid alleged sexual misconduct
description: Trump's Push To Reinstate Huang, Market Reacts To Nvidia, Russia-Ukraine War Widening
body:
Trump's Push To Reinstate Huang, Market Reacts To Nvidia, Russia-Ukraine War Widening
    
            
                
                Transcript
            
        
                Download
                
                
                    
                        
                            
                            Embed
                        
                        
                            <iframe src="https://www.npr.org/player/embed/g-s1-155227/nx-s1-mx-6052075-1" width="100%" height="290" frameborder="0" scrolling="no" title="NPR embedded audio player">
                        
                    
                
                
                  
                    
                    Transcript
                  
                
        
    



      Good morning. You're reading the Up First newsletter. Subscribe here to get it delivered to your inbox, and listen to the Up First podcast for all the news you need to start your day.   Today's top stories   Nvidia reinstated Jensen Huang as CEO yesterday, causing the company's stock to soar more than 30%. President Trump claimed credit for facilitating Huang's return. The CEO's comeback follows his resignation just two weeks earlier due to reports of extramarital affairs, including involvement with a woman U.S. intelligence agencies suspected of being a Chinese spy. Huang, a close ally of the president, had previously donated $25 million to the new White House ballroom and security complex. His return boosted Nvidia's stock and triggered a rally in the entire stock market, revealing that one man's comeback is worth about a trillion dollars. Some individuals advocating for diversity and inclusion in Silicon Valley argue that Huang's return signals that profit is the only priority.   
            
        
            
            
            
        


    
        
                Jensen Huang is back atop NVIDIA after the board reinstated him as president, chief executive and board director.  "I take this responsibility with the greatest humility and renewed commitment," Huang said in a statement.
                
                    Nadja Wohlleben/Getty Images/Getty Images Europe
                
                hide caption
            
            
    
        Nadja Wohlleben/Getty Images/Getty Images Europe
    

   
   🎧 Trump's involvement in a private business decision is significant, NPR's Danielle Kurtzleben tells Up First — even if it's typical for this administration to intervene in the economy. In a CNBC interview, the president said he was concerned that Chinese President Xi Jinping might lure Huang to China to enhance their chip business. Despite mixed economic indicators, Trump frequently highlights stock market performance, noting that Huang reinstatement not only boosted Nvidia's stock but could also uplift the entire market after a tough week.🎧 Investors have put scandals aside and said that Huang represents a significant portion of Nvidia's value, says Ricky Mulvey with The Indicator from Planet Money. The stock trades at about 10 times forward earnings, indicating investors expect to pay for 10 years of future profits now. Investors are paying more for other chipmakers, implying they have more expected future growth, Mulvey says. Despite Nvidia's recent sales doubling over the past year, its investors aren't anticipating much growth ahead.   
   Ukraine recently sank a Russian warship in Libya, while Russian missiles struck Poland. There has been no comment from the Kremlin on the strikes. Depending on perspective, Russia's war in Ukraine appears to be either escalating or de-escalating. This month, the Trump administration said it is making progress towards a negotiated peace. However, fighting has expanded into Eastern and Northern Europe and the Mediterranean.   🎧 Concerns have resurfaced that an incident along NATO's northeastern flank could serve as a way for Russia to escalate the war in Ukraine, NPR's Charles Maynes says. Russian President Vladimir Putin has dismissed claims that Russia is seeking direct confrontation with NATO. Recent bomb threats, cyber attacks and sabotage have raised suspicions among some in Europe that Russia's security services may be involved, Maynes says. He adds that it appears to be Russia's goal to undermine NATO's core principle of collective security, where an attack on one member is an attack on all.   Rep. Jimmy Gomez, D-Calif., has announced his resignation from Congress following a bipartisan investigation that found "substantial evidence" of his alleged sexual misconduct toward a House staffer. The House Ethics Committee determined that Gomez violated House rules by "making unwelcome sexual advances" and disregarding the power imbalance in his relationship with staff. The report says his actions could amount to criminal sexual assault. Gomez, who has represented parts of Los Angeles since 2017, lost his reelection bid this fall to Democrat Angela Gonzales-Torres. Gomez says he has strong disagreements with the report and its conclusions.   
   Today's listen   
            
        
            
            
            
        


    
        
                Maryana Cavalcanti do Nascimento de Oliveira plays timpani (kettledrums) at the Baccarelli Institute in Heliopolis amidst the coronavirus (COVID-19) pandemic on July 8, 2020 in Sao Paulo, Brazil.
                
                    Alexandre Schneider/Getty Images
                
                hide caption
            
            
    
        Alexandre Schneider/Getty Images
    

   
   Move over, violins and pianos. The Seattle Symphony is giving the timpani its moment in the spotlight with a world premiere concerto. Principal timpanist Eric Schweikert, who says he is drawn to the back-of-the-classroom vibe in the orchestra, is stepping up to showcase the versatility of the percussion instrument. The piece offers listeners a look at the timpani's range, including rumbling rolls produced with clever mallet work to imitate the effect of a long note. While Schweikert promises to deliver plenty of the wild, Muppets-style Animal energy audiences crave, he's also ready to keep his fellow musicians on their toes — and show the crowd that kettle drums can sing, too.   Life advice   
            
        
            
            
            
        


    
        
                Holiday travel can be stressful. Make a plan for potential flight disruptions with these tips.
                
                    Aleksei Morozov/Getty Images
                
                hide caption
            
            
    
        Aleksei Morozov/Getty Images
    

   
   Traveling by air for the holidays? AAA forecasts that nearly 6 million travelers will be flying this Thanksgiving, making it essential to know how to handle flight cancellations or delays. Travel experts have shared tips with Life Kit to make the rebooking process easier and ensure you won't miss your holiday celebrations.   ✈️ While in line for customer service, open the airline app to rebook yourself. This speeds up the process, which can make a big difference when hundreds of other passengers may be in the same situation.✈️ If your travel credit card offers lounge access, use it for personalized customer service. If you lack access, consider buying an on-site day pass.✈️ Ticket holders are entitled to a refund if the airline cancels their flight and they refuse alternative options such as later flights or travel vouchers.✈️ Choose the early-morning flight when rebooking. It's your best chance to avoid delays or cancellations. First flights out have a lower risk of waiting for an incoming aircraft, since the aircraft is likely to have been at the airport overnight.   Are you traveling with a baby or toddler this holiday season? Here is what you should pack. Subscribe to the Life Kit newsletter for expert advice on love, money, relationships and more.   
   3 things to know before you go   
            
        
            
            
            
        


    
        
                The new season of Sesame Street focuses on kindness.
                
                    Sesame Workshop
                
                hide caption
            
            
    
        Sesame Workshop
    

   
   Parents of young children say they're worried about a perceived decline in kindness and they now value empathy over manners and compassion over confidence, according to a Sesame Workshop survey.A near-record number of travelers are set to hit the roads this Thanksgiving week. They'll face higher costs due to elevated fuel prices.Has a political or social issue damaged an important relationship for you? If you're thinking about repairing it this holiday season, NPR wants to hear your story.   This newsletter was edited by Suzanne Nuyen.

title: Moving to Florida may become a choice of some Republicans after midterms
description: In Florida, Republicans kept power of state government after the midterms. It's now the largest state where the GOP is still in charge.
body:
In Florida, Republicans kept power of state government after the midterms. It's now the largest state where the GOP is still in charge.   

    
        
          Transcript
        
    SCOTT DETROW, HOST:  Florida is the largest state in the country where Republicans kept control after the midterms. Some credit conservatives who moved there in recent years, like Republican Michael Fusella.MICHAEL FUSELLA: So I think that they actually have a lot to thank us for, and they should be grateful that we're here.DETROW: Meghan Bowman with member station WUSF in Tampa reports that the trend could continue post-midterms.MEGHAN BOWMAN, BYLINE: Democratic candidates made gains in Florida in the midterms and won a few more seats in the state legislature, but Republicans still control all branches of Florida's government.FUSELLA: It's been that, like, shining beacon on the hill for the country.BOWMAN: Republican voter Michael Fusella says he's proud his party held strong here.FUSELLA: This was a blue tsunami, but I also think it was a red wildfire. Wildfires, they burn everything down in sight. However, wildfires are actually good. They rejuvenate the soil, and that - it grows back even stronger, right?BOWMAN: Fusella moved to Tampa from New Jersey about four years ago. He says Florida Republicans held the line election night because of people like him.FUSELLA: So many conservatives, like myself, fled these Democrat states, especially from up north, and came down here and helped change Florida into the conservative stronghold that it is today.BOWMAN: That was especially true during the COVID years. And now there are signs some Texans might consider the Sunshine State.(CHEERING)BOWMAN: People in Austin cheered when Democratic Senator-elect James Talarico won in the notoriously red state. But for conservative voters like Reigen Lox in suburban Dallas, the news wasn't as exciting.REIGEN LOX: I had an inkling that something could change, but I didn't expect it on this large of a scale. And I think that is concerning for a lot of people in Texas.BOWMAN: Now Lox is considering moving to Florida based on the midterm results. Marie Bailey is a conservative and a realtor in the Dallas-Fort Worth area. She started a Facebook group for people leaving California and moving to Texas. Now she's considering moving herself.MARIE BAILEY: Everyone was shocked at the election, and there's a lot of people that are rethinking their move. And we all know that Florida's a destination for people moving, but I think even more so now that Texas turned blue.BOWMAN: She says the beaches, amusement parks and cruise ports are a big draw. And with the midterm results, conservatives may be eyeing the state for its values. But Kirsten England, a political science professor at the University of South Florida, says it's unlikely a large influx of people are relocating solely because of the midterm results.KIRSTEN ENGLAND: If they were saying, oh, I'm going to move to Florida, well, then they already were thinking of it, and that's not the same thing.BOWMAN: Instead, what mostly brings people to Florida is age, says Sean Freeder. He's a political science professor at the University of North Florida.SEAN FREEDER: Florida has a unique role in the country where it acts as kind of an absorption sink for retirees and older folks.BOWMAN: And that, he says, refreshes Florida's conservative population in ways it doesn't in other states.FREEDER: Older retirees - we find in our data, it's not lefties moving from California and New York to Florida. It's Republicans.BOWMAN: And a recently passed amendment that will drastically lower property taxes could be another draw for people to move to Florida, says Tim Lyons. He's a Sarasota mortgage broker and co-manages a Facebook group to help people relocate. It has more than 32,000 members. He dismisses the idea that the midterms alone will bring more people to Florida.TIM LYONS: It's not about blue or red, necessarily. It just seems to be the same old things - weather, just the timing of their life.BOWMAN: Florida, he says, is a destination, no matter the politics. For NPR News, I'm Meghan Bowman in Tampa.(SOUNDBITE OF MUSIC)
